title: Capstone: your campaign plan
summary: Build a full campaign plan end to end, from offer and geo to tracking, budget, rules, creatives and reporting, then review it like a manager and turn it into a 30-day schedule. It brings every module of VooSquare Academy into one plan you can actually run.

lessons.title: Build your campaign plan
objectives: By the end you can write the offer, geo, source, funnel, tracking and creative parts of a campaign plan.
You can set a target CPA from the payout and your margin.
You can build a planning funnel with assumptions you will later test.

steps.p: A campaign plan is every important decision written down before you spend. It forces you to think through the offer, the people, the path and the numbers. It also gives you something to measure results against, so you learn from every test.

d.b: A plan is decisions written down before money moves
d.s: Write it, test it, learn from it

steps.say: A campaign plan is every important decision written down before money moves. It forces you to think through the offer, the people, the path and the numbers. And it gives you something to measure results against, so you learn from every test. Write it, test it, learn from it.

steps.p: Every plan in this capstone has these six parts, in this order. Each part depends on the ones before it. This lesson covers the first three; the next lesson covers budget, rules and reporting.
steps.say: Every plan in this capstone has six parts, in this order. Follow the flow: offer and geo, source and funnel, tracking, budget and rules, creatives, and reporting. Each part depends on the ones before it. This lesson covers the first three, and the next lesson covers budget, rules and reporting.

steps.p: Example only. We will build one full plan through this module so every number connects. Write the same facts for your own offer, copied from the offer page and confirmed with your network manager.
steps.say: Here's our example plan, and it's an example only. We'll build this one plan through the whole module, so every number connects. Read down the table. Trading, on C P A. A licensed broker paying forty dollars per F T D, that's first time deposit. A fifty dollar minimum first deposit as the baseline. Kenya as the geo. A cap of fifty F T Ds a week. Paid monthly, net fifteen. And about ninety percent approval history. Write the same facts for your own offer, confirmed with your network manager.

steps.p: The offer line of your plan is only as good as the partner behind it. Compare a few before you choose. Licence, accepted geos, baseline, approval history and payment terms matter more than the headline payout.

d.note: Look for licensed brokers that accept your geo, with baseline, approval and payment terms in writing.

steps.p: Trading is regulated. Before you plan a single ad, confirm the broker may accept customers from the geo and that you may advertise it there. Financial ads usually need platform authorization too. Full detail: Compliance for finance, trading and gambling offers module.

d.text: Check the local regulator (for Kenya, at the time of writing, the Capital Markets Authority) and the platform's financial services ad policy before running. If either says no, the plan stops here.

steps.say: Check regulation before anything else. Trading is regulated. Before you plan a single ad, confirm the broker may accept customers from the geo, and that you may advertise it there. Financial ads usually need platform authorization too. Read the warning: check the local regulator, for Kenya at the time of writing that's the Capital Markets Authority, and the platform's financial services ad policy. If either says no, the plan stops here.

steps.p: Your target CPA is the most you will pay per FTD and still keep your planned margin. Start from the payout you expect to be paid, then remove the margin you need to cover overheads and profit.
steps.more: Example, why 30%? From the Money and unit economics module: overheads per FTD might be about $7.50 and you also need profit and a safety margin for rejections. At $28 CPA, media margin is $12 per FTD. After $7.50 overheads, about $4.50 per FTD is profit. If your approval rate is 90%, effective payout is $36 and margin falls to $8, leaving only $0.50 after overheads. That is why the target must be checked against real approval rates in the review lesson.
steps.say: Your target C P A is the most you'll pay per F T D and still keep your planned margin. Follow the formula. Start from the forty dollar payout, keep a thirty percent margin, and your target is twenty eight dollars. Why thirty percent? Overheads per F T D might be about seven fifty, and you also need profit and a safety margin for rejections. And at ninety percent approval, the margin shrinks a lot, which is why the review lesson checks the target against real approval rates.

steps.p: Example choices with a reason for each. Writing the reason down matters, because when results come in you will know exactly which assumption to question first.
d: Why Telegram|educate and build trust before deposit
Message match|ad, lander and channel say the same thing
steps.say: Here are the example choices for source and funnel, each with a reason. Look at the cards. The source is Meta, broad audience, in Kenya. The funnel goes ad, then prelander, then Telegram, then broker sign-up. Telegram is there to educate and build trust before a deposit. There are English and Swahili versions. And message match, so the ad, lander and channel all say the same thing. Writing the reason down tells you which assumption to question first when results come in.

steps.p: Planning assumptions for the first test, not promises. At an example $0.25 cost per click, 2,000 clicks cost $500. If 20 people make a first deposit, CPA is $25, under the $28 target.
steps.more: Example rates behind the funnel: 85% of clicks load the lander, 29% of lander views join Telegram (500 ÷ 1,700), 24% of joins register (120 ÷ 500) and about 17% of registrations deposit (20 ÷ 120). Every one of these is a guess until the test runs. Write them down anyway: when the test ends you compare each real rate with its guess and find the weakest stage in minutes.
steps.say: Here's the example planning funnel. These are planning assumptions for the first test, not promises. At an example twenty five cents per click, two thousand clicks cost five hundred dollars. Watch the funnel narrow: seventeen hundred lander views, five hundred Telegram joins, a hundred and twenty registrations, and twenty first deposits. That's a C P A of twenty five dollars, under the twenty eight dollar target. Every rate is a guess until the test runs, so write them down and compare later.

steps.h: The example funnel as a system
steps.p: The same plan as a map of what happens to one person and to the data. Every arrow is a step you will test before launch. Every data node is where a number in your plan will come from.
steps.say: Here's the same plan as a map of what happens to one person, and to the data. Follow the arrows. The Meta ad leads to the prelander, then the Telegram channel and welcome bot, then broker sign-up. The F T D fires a network postback to your tracker, which sends an event through the Conversions A P I back to Meta, so it can optimise. Every arrow is a step you'll test before launch. Every data node is where a number in your plan comes from.

steps.p: Decide what each event is, where it is recorded and where it is sent. Test every row with a real click and a test sign-up before launch, because broken tracking makes every later decision a guess. Full setup: Tracking setup lab module.
steps.say: Decide what each event is, where it's recorded and where it's sent. Read the table. Clicks are recorded with U T Ms and a click I D, and go to the tracker. Telegram joins come from the join tracker, sent to Meta through the Conversions A P I. Registrations and first deposits come from network postbacks, and deposits go to both the tracker and Meta. Test every row with a real click and a test sign-up before launch. Broken tracking makes every later decision a guess.

steps.p: Start with a small, structured set so the test teaches you something. Each creative must pass the platform's policy and your own honesty check before it runs.
d: English and Swahili versions, checked by a fluent speaker
No income claims; clear risk wording
Every ad checked against current ad policy
A short brief written for each angle
steps.say: Start with a small, structured set of creatives, so the test teaches you something. Three angles times two formats gives six ads. English and Swahili versions, checked by a fluent speaker. No income claims, and clear risk wording. Every ad checked against current ad policy. And a short brief written for each angle. Each creative must pass both the platform's policy and your own honesty check before it runs.

steps.p: Angles are the reasons someone might care. These are honest angles for a trading education funnel. None of them promise money, because the plan must pass both platform policy and your own standards.
d: Learn first|free lessons before you trade
Know the tools|how the platform works
Risk first|how to protect your money
steps.say: Angles are the reasons someone might care. Look at these honest angles for a trading education funnel. Learn first, with free lessons before you trade. Know the tools, how the platform works. Learn together, a community of beginners. And risk first, how to protect your money. Notice none of them promise money, because the plan has to pass both platform policy and your own standards.

steps.p: These are the planning mistakes managers see most often. Each one looks small on paper and becomes expensive once money is moving. Check your own plan against them before the next lesson.
d: Offer chosen by payout alone|check licence, geo, approval, terms
Target from headline payout|use approval rate too
Tracking set up later|test it before launch
Ten angles at once|3 angles × 2 formats
Regulation skipped|check law and authorization first
steps.say: These are the planning mistakes managers see most often. Look at the cards. Choosing an offer by payout alone, instead of checking licence, geo, approval and terms. Setting the target from the headline payout, without the approval rate. Setting tracking up later, instead of testing before launch. Running ten angles at once, instead of three angles times two formats. And skipping regulation. Each looks small on paper, and gets expensive once money is moving.

lessons.say_intro: This is the capstone, where everything comes together in one campaign plan. In this lesson you'll write the offer, geo, source, funnel, tracking and creative parts, and set a target C P A, cost per acquisition, from your payout and margin.

Your task: write those parts of your own one-page plan, including your target C P A and planning funnel. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Budget, rules and reporting
objectives: By the end you can size a test budget from your target CPA.
You can write numeric kill, hold and scale rules.
You can plan the cash a campaign needs and the reports that track it.

steps.h: Budget the test, then the cash
steps.p: There are two budgets in every plan. The test budget is what you will spend to learn whether the campaign works. The cash plan is what you need to carry the campaign until payouts arrive if it does work.

d.b: Budget the test, then budget the cash
d.s: One answers 'does it work', the other 'can I afford it'

steps.say: Every plan has two budgets. The test budget is what you'll spend to learn whether the campaign works. The cash plan is what you need to carry the campaign until payouts arrive, if it does work. One answers, does it work. The other answers, can I afford it. Budget the test first, then the cash.

steps.p: A common starting rule is to give each ad set a daily budget near your target CPA, and to run long enough to see several conversions. Rough guide only; adjust to your geo, vertical and account history.
steps.say: Here's how to size the test. Follow the formula: number of ad sets, times the daily budget each, times the number of days, equals your test budget. A common starting rule is to give each ad set a daily budget near your target C P A, and to run long enough to see several conversions. It's a rough guide only, so adjust it to your geo, vertical and account history.

steps.p: Example from our plan: three ad sets, one per angle, each at $28 a day, the target CPA. Run for seven days before judging, applying the kill rules daily to stop clear losers early.

d.text: Example: 3 × $28 × 7 = $588 test budget, about $84 a day.

steps.say: Here's the worked example from our plan. Three ad sets, one per angle, each at twenty eight dollars a day, which is the target C P A. Run for seven days before judging, while applying the kill rules daily to stop clear losers early. So three times twenty eight times seven is a five hundred and eighty eight dollar test budget, about eighty four dollars a day.

steps.p: Starting rules from the Budget and kill rules module, for a $28 target. Break-even is $40 × 90% approval = $36, below 1.5 × $28 = $42, so the CPA kill line is $36. Check from the top; the first true row wins. Count network-confirmed FTDs only.
steps.more: Why these numbers? 2 × $28 = $56, so an ad set with no FTD by $56 is paused. 3 × $28 = $84 is the spend at which CPA is judged. 0.8 × $28 = $22.40 is the scale line. Keep means the ad set is on target and stays as it is. Hold means there is not enough data to decide, so you change nothing until the next checkpoint. Adapt these to your vertical once you have your own data.
steps.say: Here are the starting rules for a twenty eight dollar target. Break-even is forty dollars times ninety percent approval, so thirty six, which is below one point five times target. So the kill line is thirty six. Read the table from the top. Kill at zero F T Ds, first time deposits, by fifty six dollars spend. Kill at eighty four spend with C P A above thirty six. Scale twenty percent with three plus F T Ds at twenty two forty or less. Keep between twenty two forty and twenty eight. Anything else is hold. Count network-confirmed F T Ds only.

steps.p: Try it. Example: target $28, break-even $36. An ad set has spent $90 over three days with 3 network-confirmed FTDs. Work out the CPA, check the rules from the top and make the call.

d.task: Example: $90 spent, 3 confirmed FTDs, $28 target, 3 days. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Now try it yourself. In this example, the target is twenty eight dollars and break-even is thirty six. An ad set has spent ninety dollars over three days, with three network-confirmed F T Ds. Work out the C P A, check the rules from the top, and make the call: kill, hold or scale. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: The daily checkpoint, click by click
steps.p: Do this at the same time each day. Names and screens change; check the current Ads Manager and your network panel. The order matters: network numbers first, then the rules, then any change in the ad platform.

steps.title: Pull confirmed FTDs
steps.text: Open the network report for today and note confirmed FTDs per ad set, using your sub IDs.

steps.title: Fill the daily sheet
steps.text: Enter spend from the ad platform and FTDs from the network.

steps.title: Apply the rules
steps.text: Check each row from the top of the rule card and write the decision.

steps.title: Make the change
steps.text: Raise A from $28 to $33.60 a day, and pause C. Leave B alone.

steps.say: Here's the daily checkpoint, click by click. Do it at the same time each day. Tap Next to follow each step. First, pull confirmed F T Ds per ad set from the network report, using your sub I Ds. Second, fill the daily sheet with spend from the ad platform and F T Ds from the network. Third, apply the rules to each row from the top of the rule card. In the example, A scales, B keeps, C is killed. Fourth, make the change: raise A to thirty three sixty a day, pause C, and leave B alone.

steps.p: Guardrails protect the whole plan, not single ad sets. They catch problems the per-ad-set rules miss, such as an offer hitting its cap or an account warning.
d: Daily stop-loss|total loss limit per day
Weekly spend cap|never above the cash plan
Offer cap|50 FTDs a week; stop before it
steps.say: Guardrails protect the whole plan, not single ad sets. Look at the cards. A daily stop-loss, a total loss limit per day. A weekly spend cap that never goes above the cash plan. The offer cap, fifty F T Ds a week, so stop before it. Account health, checking warnings every day. And a weekly review of rejections. These catch problems the per ad set rules miss.

steps.p: When an ad set or account hits a limit, the answer is the rules, not a way around them. Spreading spend over extra accounts to dodge limits or a restriction breaks platform policy. See the Ad account bans module for the honest response.

d.text: Never open or borrow extra ad accounts to get around spend limits, restrictions or bans. Follow platform policy and appeal through official channels.

steps.say: Guardrails never include workarounds. When an ad set or account hits a limit, the answer is the rules, not a way around them. Spreading spend over extra accounts to dodge limits or a restriction breaks platform policy. Read the warning: never open or borrow extra ad accounts to get around spend limits, restrictions or bans. Follow platform policy, and appeal through official channels.

steps.p: Example: if the test works, total spend grows. Week one $84 a day, week two $140 a day, then $200 a day from day 15. The first payout, for the launch month, lands about 45 days after launch.
steps.more: Example, the maths. Week one: 7 × $84 = $588. Week two: 7 × $140 = $980. Days 15 to 45: 31 days × $200 = $6,200. Total spend before the first payout: $7,768. With a 20% buffer kept on top, the plan needs about $9,700 of cleared cash. If you only have $5,000, the plan must ramp more slowly or cap at a lower daily spend. This is the cash rule from the Money and unit economics module applied to a real plan. The ramp only happens if the rules allow it: +20% steps on winners every 48 hours or more, plus new ad sets that each start under the kill rules.

d.text: Example: $588 + $980 + (31 days × $200 = $6,200) = $7,768 needed before the first payout, plus a buffer.

steps.say: Here's the worked example of the cash plan. If the test works, spend grows. Week one at eighty four dollars a day is five hundred and eighty eight. Week two at a hundred and forty a day is nine hundred and eighty. Then two hundred a day from day fifteen to day forty five, which is six thousand two hundred. The first payout lands about forty five days after launch. So you need seven thousand seven hundred and sixty eight dollars before the first payout, plus a buffer.

steps.p: Illustration of the example cash plan. The test is a small part of the total. Most of the cash need comes from scaling a winner before the first payout, which is exactly when operators run out of money.
steps.say: This illustration shows where the cash goes. Look at the bars. The week one test is a small part of the total. Week two is a bit more. But the big bar, days fifteen to forty five, is where most of the cash goes, from scaling a winner before the first payout. That's exactly when operators run out of money.

steps.p: The number to confirm before launch. If you do not have it in cleared cash, change the plan now, by ramping slower or capping spend, rather than discovering the gap in week four.

d.label: cleared cash needed, including a 20% buffer

steps.say: Here's the number to confirm before launch: nine thousand seven hundred and ten dollars of cleared cash, including a twenty percent buffer. In this example, that's seven thousand seven hundred and sixty eight divided by point eight. If you don't have it in cleared cash, change the plan now, by ramping slower or capping spend, rather than discovering the gap in week four.

steps.p: Reports turn data into decisions. Each one has a rhythm, a short list of numbers and a decision it supports. Name who writes each report, and when, in the plan itself.

rows: Iterate and set next week's cap

steps.say: Reports turn data into decisions. Read the table. The daily report covers spend, F T Ds, C P A and account health, and supports applying the kill and scale rules. The weekly report covers creatives, funnel rates, approvals and cash, so you iterate and set next week's cap. The monthly report covers the P and L, cohort L T V, that's lifetime value, and payouts, to change targets and budget. Name who writes each report, and when, in the plan itself.

steps.p: Illustration of a daily report chart during the first week. Early CPA is noisy and high, then settles as the platform learns and weak ads are paused. Judge the trend over several days, not one point.
steps.say: This illustration shows a daily report chart in the first week. Watch the actual C P A line. It starts high and noisy, around forty five dollars on day one, then settles toward the flat twenty eight dollar target line, reaching about twenty five by day seven, as the platform learns and weak ads are paused. Judge the trend over several days, not one point.

steps.p: Five lines, sent at the same time every day. It takes ten minutes and keeps you, a partner or a manager looking at the same facts before any decision.
d: Spend today and month to date
FTDs and CPA by ad set
steps.say: Here's the daily report template, five lines sent at the same time every day. Spend today and month to date. F T Ds and C P A by ad set. The rules applied, and why. Any account or policy warnings. And any change to the cash forecast. It takes ten minutes, and it keeps you, a partner or a manager looking at the same facts before any decision.

steps.p: These are the rule-breaking habits that cost new operators most. The rule card only works if it is applied the same way every day, at the same time, with the same numbers.
d: Scaling twice in a day|+20% every 48 hours at most
Reviving a killed ad set|launch a new one instead
Ignoring the cash plan|check it before each step
Reports nobody reads|named owner, fixed time
steps.say: These are the rule-breaking habits that cost new operators most. Look at the cards. Judging on platform conversions, instead of network-confirmed only. Scaling twice in a day, instead of twenty percent every forty eight hours at most. Reviving a killed ad set, instead of launching a new one. Ignoring the cash plan, instead of checking it before each step. And reports nobody reads, instead of a named owner and a fixed time. The rule card only works if you apply it the same way every day.

quiz.q: Example: 4 ad sets at $30 a day for 6 days. What is the test budget?
Example rules: target $28, kill line $36. An ad set has 6 network-confirmed FTDs at $43 CPA. What do you do?
options: Pause it; CPA is above the kill line
Double the budget to lower CPA
quiz.why: Spend is $258, above 3 × $28 = $84, and the $43 CPA is above the $36 kill line (lower of $42 and the $36 break-even), so the kill rule applies.

quiz.q: Example: ramp spend totals $7,000 before the first payout and you keep a 20% buffer. What cleared cash do you need?
quiz.why: $7,000 ÷ 0.8 = $8,750, so that $7,000 is 80% and the buffer is 20%.

quiz.q: Which decision does the weekly report support?
options: Iterating creatives and setting next week's spend cap
quiz.why: Weekly reports look at creatives, funnel rates, approvals and cash to plan the next week.

quiz.q: Your offer cap is 50 FTDs a week and you reached 46 by Thursday. What does the guardrail say?
options: Slow or stop spend before the cap and ask the network about room
quiz.why: FTDs over the cap may not be paid, so slow down and confirm with the network.

lessons.title: Review the plan like a manager
objectives: By the end you can review a campaign plan with a manager-style checklist.
You can stress test a plan's numbers against realistic bad cases.
You can approve, fix or reject a plan with clear reasons.

steps.p: A manager does not ask whether the plan could work. They ask what breaks first, how much it costs when it does and whether the plan already has an answer. Learn to ask those questions of your own plans.

d.b: A manager asks what breaks first
d.s: Then checks the plan already has an answer

steps.say: A manager doesn't ask whether a plan could work. They ask what breaks first, how much it costs when it does, and whether the plan already has an answer. That's the habit to build. Learn to ask those questions of your own plans.

steps.p: Run through these first. A plan that fails any of them is not ready, however good the creatives or the funnel look. Each item should have a clear yes, with the evidence written in the plan.
d: Offer is legal for the geo and ads are authorised
Target CPA comes from real payout, approval and margin
Tracking tested end to end with a real conversion
Kill, hold and scale rules written with numbers
Cleared cash covers spend to first payout plus buffer
Retention plan respects consent and opt-outs
steps.say: Run through the foundations first. Is the offer legal for the geo, with ads authorised? Does the target C P A, cost per acquisition, come from the real payout, approval and margin? Is tracking tested end to end with a real conversion? Are kill, hold and scale rules written with numbers? Does cleared cash cover spend to first payout, plus a buffer? And does the retention plan respect consent and opt-outs? Each needs a clear yes, with evidence in the plan.

steps.p: Then check the details that usually cause trouble in week two or three. These are smaller items, but each one has stopped real campaigns that looked fine on day one.
d: Offer cap and payment terms written down
A named owner for each report
steps.say: Then check the details that usually cause trouble in week two or three. Is every creative policy-checked and honest? Are the offer cap and payment terms written down? Is there a named owner for each report? Is a backup creative batch ready? And is account health checked daily? These are smaller items, but each one has stopped real campaigns that looked fine on day one.

steps.p: Use this to score each part of the plan quickly. One red flag in a foundation section means the plan goes back for fixes. Green flags are what good plans look like.
steps.say: Use this table to score each part of the plan quickly. Read across. For the offer, the red flag is network said it's fine, and the green flag is terms and licence checked. Target C P A based on the headline payout is red, using the approval rate is green. Untested tracking is red. Rules judged by feel are red. Cash not calculated is red. And income claims in creatives are red. One red flag in a foundation section means the plan goes back for fixes.

steps.p: Ask what happens if things go worse than planned. Each line is a realistic bad case. A good plan has a written response for each, decided before it happens rather than in a panic.
steps.say: Now the stress tests. Ask what happens if things go worse than planned. Read the table. If C P C, cost per click, is thirty percent higher, C P A goes from twenty five to thirty two fifty, so you'd test new creatives and the lander. If approval falls to eighty percent, effective payout is thirty two, so you review traffic quality. A late payout grows the cash gap. A restricted account stops spend, so you appeal and follow policy. A cap reached early means you pause and ask for more.

steps.p: Example from our plan: payout $40, planned CPA $25. If clicks cost 30% more, CPA rises to $32.50. If approval falls to 80%, each reported FTD is worth $32. If both happen together, the plan loses money.
steps.more: Example, each case. Base: $40 − $25 = $15 media margin per FTD. CPC up 30%: CPA $25 × 1.3 = $32.50, margin $40 − $32.50 = $7.50. Approval at 80%: $32 − $25 = $7. Both together: $32 − $32.50 = −$0.50. With overheads near $7.50 per FTD, even the single bad cases leave almost nothing. The manager's fix might be a lower target CPA, a stricter kill rule, or a second offer with better approval.

d.text: Example: $40 × 80% = $32 effective payout. $32 − $32.50 = −$0.50 per FTD before overheads.

steps.say: Here's the stress maths from our example. The payout is forty dollars and the planned C P A is twenty five, so the media margin is fifteen dollars per F T D, first time deposit. If clicks cost thirty percent more, C P A rises to thirty two fifty. If approval falls to eighty percent, each reported F T D is worth thirty two. And if both happen together, thirty two minus thirty two fifty is minus fifty cents per F T D, before overheads. The plan loses money.

steps.p: Illustration of the example. Media margin per FTD before overheads, in each case. The combined case falls below zero, so the plan needs a written response for it before launch.
steps.say: Here's that example as bars, showing media margin per F T D before overheads. The base case is fifteen dollars. C P C up thirty percent leaves seven fifty. Approval at eighty percent leaves seven. And both together falls below zero, to minus fifty cents. So the plan needs a written response for that combined case before launch.

steps.p: Try it. In the stress case approval falls to 80%, so effective payout is $40 × 80% = $32. You still want to keep a 30% margin. What is the most you can now pay per FTD?

d.task: Example: effective payout $32, keep 30%. What is the new maximum CPA?

steps.say: Now practise. In the stress case, approval falls to eighty percent, so effective payout is forty dollars times eighty percent, which is thirty two. You still want to keep a thirty percent margin. What's the most you can now pay per F T D? Enter the new maximum C P A. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: Common mistakes: a weak plan and a strong plan
steps.p: Both plans target the same offer. The weak one is built on hope and headline numbers. The strong one is built on checked facts and written responses. Managers approve the second kind.

b.title: Strong plan
items: Cash to first payout plus buffer

steps.say: Both of these plans target the same offer. Compare them. The weak plan uses the headline payout as its target, says tracking will be set up later, has no cash forecast, and its rules are see how it goes. The strong plan uses the approval rate in its target, tracks a test F T D before launch, forecasts cash to first payout plus a buffer, and has numeric rules and owners. Managers approve the second kind.

steps.p: Use the same order every time, whether you review your own plan or a buyer's. Writing fixes with owners and dates is what turns a review into action rather than a conversation.
steps.say: Use the same review order every time, whether it's your own plan or a buyer's. Follow the flow. Read the one-page plan. Run both checklists. Stress test the numbers. Write fixes with owners. And approve with limits. Writing fixes with owners and dates is what turns a review into action, rather than a conversation.

steps.h: Run a review, step by step
steps.p: This is the review process on a real plan document. It works the same whether you review your own plan alone or a buyer's plan with them. Give it about 45 minutes the first time.

steps.title: Read the one-page plan
steps.text: Read it end to end before judging any part. Note questions in the margin.

steps.title: Tick the foundations
steps.text: Each foundation needs a clear yes with evidence. One no sends the plan back.

blocks.label: Offer legal for geo, ads authorised
Cash covers spend to payout + buffer

steps.title: Run the stress tests
steps.text: Work out margin per FTD in each bad case and check each has a response.

steps.title: Write fixes with owners
steps.text: Every fix gets one owner and one date.

rows: Test a real FTD end to end

steps.title: Record the decision
steps.text: Choose one outcome and save the sign-off.

steps.say: Here's a review on a real plan document. Give it about forty five minutes the first time. Tap Next to follow each step. First, read the one-page plan end to end, noting questions. Here, tracking says tested, not stated. Second, tick the foundations, each needing a clear yes, and tracking isn't ticked, so one no sends it back. Third, run the stress tests and check each case has a response. Fourth, write fixes, each with one owner and one date. Fifth, record the decision and save the sign-off.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They keep reviews consistent, so two reviewers looking at the same plan reach the same decision. Write the reason next to the verdict every time.

rows: Combined stress case below zero, no response
Fix: lower target or add a response
Approve with a spend cap to first payout

steps.say: These starting rules keep reviews consistent, so two reviewers looking at the same plan reach the same decision. Read the table. Any foundation red flag, fix before launch. Any dishonest method, reject. A combined stress case below zero with no response, fix it by lowering the target or adding a response. All foundations green, approve, with a spend cap until the first payout. Write the reason next to the verdict every time.

steps.p: Every review ends with one of three decisions. Approve with limits, such as a maximum spend until the first payout. Send back with specific fixes. Or reject, with the reason written down so everyone learns from it.

d.s: Always with the reason written down

steps.say: Every review ends with one of three decisions. Approve with limits, such as a maximum spend until the first payout. Send it back with specific fixes. Or reject it, with the reason written down so everyone learns from it. Approve, fix or reject, always with the reason written down.

steps.h: Some plans are rejected whatever the numbers
steps.p: Strong numbers never excuse dishonest methods. A plan that relies on any of these is rejected outright, because it puts accounts, partners and real people at risk.

d.text: Reject any plan that uses cloaking, fake reviews, misleading or income claims, stolen creatives, bought lists or ignoring opt-outs.

steps.say: Some plans are rejected whatever the numbers. Strong numbers never excuse dishonest methods. Read the warning: reject any plan that uses cloaking, fake reviews, misleading or income claims, stolen creatives, bought lists, or ignores opt-outs. A plan like that puts accounts, partners and real people at risk.

steps.p: Reviewers make mistakes too, usually by being too kind or too quick. These are the ones that let weak plans through. Avoid them whether you review a team member or yourself.
d: Starting with creatives|start with the foundations
Approving without limits|cap spend until first payout
Fixes without owners|one owner and one date each
Waving through small policy issues|fix or reject before launch
steps.say: Reviewers make mistakes too, usually by being too kind or too quick. Look at the cards. Starting with creatives, when you should start with the foundations. Approving without limits, instead of capping spend until first payout. Writing fixes without owners, instead of one owner and one date each. And waving through small policy issues, when they should be fixed or rejected before launch.

steps.p: Dchessking on the first thing he asks when a buyer at Zedapex brings him a new campaign plan for review, before he looks at the creatives or the targeting.
steps.d: When a buyer brings me a plan, I ask one question first: what happens to this money if the payout is late? A good plan already has the answer written down.

Spend limit until first payout agreed
Owners named for reports and rules
Plan saved where the team can find it

Stress test CPC, approval rate, payout delays, account issues and caps.
Every review ends in approve with limits, fix, or reject, with reasons.

options: Approve; tracking can be fixed later
Send back to fix: test a real conversion end to end first
quiz.why: Tracking is a foundation; without it every later decision is a guess.

quiz.q: A plan shows strong ROI using a cloaked lander. What does the manager do?
quiz.why: Cloaking breaks platform rules and is never acceptable, regardless of results.

lessons.say_intro: This lesson teaches you to review a campaign plan the way a manager does. You'll run two checklists, stress test the numbers against realistic bad cases, and end with a clear decision: approve, fix or reject.
lessons.say_outro: A manager asks what breaks first: run the foundations and details checklists, stress test the numbers, write fixes with owners, and end with approve, fix or reject, with reasons and limits. Dishonest methods are rejected whatever the numbers. Your task: review your own plan with both checklists, run the five stress tests, and write at least three fixes with owners. Now take the quiz.

lessons.title: Your 30-day plan and what comes next
objectives: By the end you can turn an approved plan into a week-by-week 30-day schedule.
You can decide what to do at day 30 whether the campaign worked or not.
You can choose your next steps as an operator after VooSquare Academy.

steps.h: Thirty days, four weeks, one plan
steps.p: An approved plan becomes real through a schedule. Each week has one main job and a short list of tasks. At the end of the thirty days you will have results, data and a clear next decision, whatever happened.

d.b: Thirty days, four weeks, one plan

steps.say: An approved plan becomes real through a schedule. Thirty days, four weeks, one plan, and each week has one main job and a short list of tasks. At the end of the thirty days, you'll have results, data and a clear next decision, whatever happened.

steps.p: This structure works for most first campaigns at a new offer or geo. Do not skip ahead. Each week depends on the data the week before produced.
steps.say: Here are the four weeks. Follow the flow. Week one, set up and test. Week two, cut and iterate. Week three, scale carefully. Week four, review and retain. This structure works for most first campaigns at a new offer or geo. Don't skip ahead, because each week depends on the data the week before produced.

steps.p: The week starts with checks, not ads. Launch only once tracking and policy checks pass. Then follow the kill rules every day, even when the early numbers are exciting or worrying.
d: Days 1-2: tracking test with a real conversion
Day 2: final policy check on all ads
Day 3: launch 3 ad sets at $28 a day
Days 3-7: daily report, apply kill rules
Day 7: compare funnel rates with the plan
steps.say: Week one starts with checks, not ads. Days one and two, a tracking test with a real conversion. Day two, a final policy check on all ads. Day three, launch three ad sets at twenty eight dollars a day. Days three to seven, a daily report, applying the kill rules. And day seven, compare the funnel rates with the plan. Launch only once tracking and policy checks pass, and follow the kill rules every day, even when early numbers are exciting or worrying.

steps.p: Example of week one as calendar tasks. Each day has one main task and an owner. The first rule checkpoint comes 48 hours after launch, not on launch day, because early numbers are too thin to judge.

rows: Tracking test with a real conversion
Launch 3 ad sets at $28 a day
Compare funnel rates with the plan

steps.say: Here's week one as calendar tasks, an example where each day has one main task and an owner. Read down the table, from the tracking test on day one, through launch on day three. Notice the first rule checkpoint is on day five, forty eight hours after launch, not on launch day. That's because early numbers are too thin to judge.

steps.p: Use week one's data to remove what failed and improve what worked. Change one thing at a time where you can, so you know what caused any change in results.
d: Pause ad sets that hit kill rules
Write new creatives for the best angle
Check approval rate with the network
steps.say: Week two is cut and iterate. Use week one's data to remove what failed and improve what worked. Pause ad sets that hit kill rules. Write new creatives for the best angle. Fix the weakest funnel stage. Check the approval rate with the network. And update the cash forecast. Change one thing at a time where you can, so you know what caused any change in results.

steps.h: The day 7 review, step by step
steps.p: At the end of week one, compare what happened with what you planned. The goal is one decision for week two: which single stage or creative to change. Example numbers follow the plan from this module.

steps.title: Check each ad set
steps.text: Use network-confirmed FTDs and the rule card from the Budget and kill rules module.

steps.title: Compare funnel rates
steps.text: Put each real stage rate next to the planning funnel.

steps.title: Pick one change
steps.text: The stage furthest below plan is the one to fix first.

steps.say: Here's the day seven review, step by step. Tap Next to follow each step. First, check each ad set with network-confirmed F T Ds, first time deposits, and the rule card. In the example, A is kept at about twenty three dollars, B is on hold at thirty five, and C was killed on day five. Second, compare each real funnel rate with the plan. Lander to join came in at twenty two percent against twenty nine planned. Third, pick one change: the weakest stage, so a new lander headline, owned by you, on day nine.

steps.p: Week two asks for new creatives on the best angle. Looking at what is running in your geo helps you see which angles and formats are common. Use it for ideas only; never copy another advertiser's creative.

d.why: Spyvoo shows live ads in your geo, which helps you research angles for week two's new creatives.

steps.say: Week two asks for new creatives on the best angle. Looking at what's running in your geo helps you see which angles and formats are common. A spy tool like the one shown can help you research. Use it for ideas only, and never copy another advertiser's creative.

steps.p: Only scale what met the scale rule. Raise budgets in steps, and check the cash forecast before each one. If nothing met the rule, week three is more iteration, not scaling.
d: Raise winners about 20% when rules allow
Duplicate the best ad set to a new audience
Keep the daily stop-loss in place
steps.say: Week three is scale carefully. Raise winners about twenty percent when the rules allow. Duplicate the best ad set to a new audience. Keep the daily stop-loss in place. Watch the offer cap. And check account health daily. Only scale what met the scale rule, raise budgets in steps, and check the cash forecast before each one. If nothing met the rule, week three is more iteration, not scaling.

steps.p: The last week adds retention and the first full review. By now you have joins, registrations and some deposits. Start working the people you paid for, and measure what the month really produced.
d: Launch the welcome drip and first broadcasts
steps.say: Week four is review and retain. Launch the welcome drip and first broadcasts. Check opt-out and unsubscribe rates. Hold the first monthly review. Write down what you learned. And decide the next thirty days. By now you have joins, registrations and some deposits, so start working the people you paid for, and measure what the month really produced.

steps.p: Illustration of the example plan if the rules allow each step. Week four only reaches $240 a day if the scale rule is met. Update the cash forecast before every step.
steps.more: Example totals. Four weeks: $588 + $980 + $1,400 + $1,680 = $4,648. Days 29 and 30 at $240 add $480, so the 30-day total is $5,128. Spend continues after day 30 while you wait for the first payout around day 45, which is why the cash plan in the Budget, rules and reporting lesson covers spend to the payout date, not just the first month. The weekly figures are totals across all ad sets: winners rise in +20% steps every 48 hours or more, and new ad sets for new angles or audiences add the rest, each under the kill rules.
steps.say: This illustration shows the example weekly spend plan, if the rules allow each step. Look at the bars. Week one, five hundred and eighty eight dollars. Week two, nine hundred and eighty. Week three, fourteen hundred. Week four, sixteen hundred and eighty at two hundred and forty a day. But week four only reaches that if the scale rule is met. Update the cash forecast before every step.

steps.p: Targets are your own plan choices, not benchmarks. Write them before launch and review them on day 30. Missing a target is information, not failure, as long as you learn why.

rows: Daily and weekly sent on time

steps.say: Here are example thirty day targets. Read the table. C P A, cost per acquisition, at or under twenty eight dollars, checked daily. Approval rate ninety percent or higher, checked weekly. A cash buffer never below twenty percent. No rising trend in unsubscribes. And daily and weekly reports sent on time. These are your own plan choices, not benchmarks. Missing a target is information, not failure, as long as you learn why.

steps.p: Starting rules from the Budget and kill rules module, applied to this plan with a $28 target and $36 kill line. Count only network-confirmed FTDs and adapt the numbers once you have your own data.

rows: No increases; cut to the ceiling

steps.say: Here are the starting rules for the thirty days, with a twenty eight dollar target and a thirty six dollar kill line. Zero F T Ds at fifty six dollars spend, kill the ad set. Spend of eighty four or more with C P A over thirty six, kill. Three plus F T Ds at twenty two forty or less, raise twenty percent, every forty eight hours at most. Test budget spent with nothing kept, stop and revise. Cash buffer under twenty percent, no increases. Count only network-confirmed F T Ds.

steps.p: Most first 30-day plans go wrong in the same few ways. None of them are about talent. They are about skipping steps when results feel exciting or disappointing.
d: Launching before the tracking test|test on days 1-2
Scaling on one cheap FTD|wait for 3+ confirmed
Changing many things at once|one change at a time
Retention left for later|start the drip in week 4
No day-30 review booked|put it in the calendar now
steps.say: Most first thirty day plans go wrong in the same few ways, and none of them are about talent. Look at the cards. Launching before the tracking test. Scaling on one cheap F T D, instead of waiting for three plus confirmed. Changing many things at once. Leaving retention for later. And not booking the day thirty review. They're about skipping steps when results feel exciting or disappointing.

steps.p: Both outcomes are useful if you recorded the data. A working campaign moves to steady scaling. A failed test goes back to the plan, with a specific change, not a bigger budget.

a.title: If it worked
items: Add a second angle or audience

b.title: If it did not
items: Keep the loss inside the test budget

steps.say: At day thirty, there are two outcomes. Compare the columns. If it worked, scale by the rules, add a second angle or audience, start cohort L T V, lifetime value, tracking, and ask about better payment terms. If it didn't, find the weakest funnel stage, change the offer, angle or lander, keep the loss inside the test budget, and never double down to recover. Both outcomes are useful if you recorded the data.

steps.p: Most first tests at a new offer or geo do not work. That is normal. The test budget was set so that a loss teaches you without hurting the business. Doubling spend to win it back is how small losses become large ones.

d.text: If week one fails the kill rules, stop and revise the plan. Do not raise budgets to recover a loss.

steps.say: A failed test is tuition. Most first tests at a new offer or geo don't work, and that's normal. The test budget was set so that a loss teaches you without hurting the business. Doubling spend to win it back is how small losses become large ones. Read the warning: if week one fails the kill rules, stop and revise the plan. Don't raise budgets to recover a loss.

d: Second geo|repeat the plan in a new market
Team|train a junior buyer with your SOPs
Community|share lessons and learn from others

Pick one at a time. Each builds on honest methods, written plans, numeric rules and cash discipline.

exam.q: Your offer pays $60 per FTD with an 85% approval rate. You want a 30% margin on effective payout. What target CPA do you set?
You plan a trading offer for Ghana. The network says ads are fine. What do you do before planning creatives?
options: Confirm with the local regulator's rules and the platform's financial ads policy, including authorization
Run a small test to see if ads get rejected
exam.why: Regulated verticals need your own check of local law and platform authorization; a network's word is not enough.

exam.q: Planning funnel: 3,000 clicks at $0.20, 24 FTDs expected. Target CPA $28. Is the plan inside target?
Payout $50, approval rate 80%, target CPA $30. An ad set has spent $100 for 2 network-confirmed FTDs. What do the starting rules say?
options: Kill; spend is past 3 × target and the $50 CPA is above the $40 kill line
Keep; it is within the payout
exam.why: Break-even is $50 × 80% = $40, below 1.5 × $30 = $45, so the kill line is $40. Spend $100 ≥ $90 (3 × target) and CPA $50 > $40, so kill.

exam.q: Ramp spend before the first payout is $9,600. You keep a 20% buffer. You have $10,000 cleared. What does the review say?
options: Fix: $12,000 is needed with buffer; ramp slower or cap spend
exam.why: $9,600 ÷ 0.8 = $12,000 needed; $10,000 is short, so the ramp must change.

exam.q: Payout $40, planned CPA $25. CPC rises 20% and approval falls to 90%. What is the media margin per FTD?
An ad set has spent $60 with no FTDs and no registrations. Target CPA is $28 and the kill rule is 2× target. What do you do?
options: Pause it; it passed $56 with no signal
Raise budget to give it a chance
exam.why: The rule is 2 × $28 = $56; it passed that with no signal, so pause.

exam.q: A buyer's plan has numeric rules, tested tracking and a cash forecast, but creatives say "Earn $200 a day". What is the decision?
options: Approve if the ads get through review
Send back: income claims must be removed before approval
exam.why: Misleading income claims break policy and honesty rules; the plan cannot run with them.

exam.q: Day 30: CPA averaged $34 against a $28 target, approval 92%, payout $40. What is the best next step?
options: Revise: fix the weakest funnel stage or creative before scaling
exam.why: CPA is above target but below the $36.80 break-even ($40 × 92%), so no kill rule fires; improve the plan before scaling rather than raising spend.

exam.q: Week four retention: your welcome drip's unsubscribe rate rises each send. What do you do?
options: Send more often to reach people
Reduce frequency and review content for that segment
Buy a list to replace leavers
exam.why: A rising unsubscribe rate means the messages or frequency do not suit the segment; fix it and keep opt-outs working.
